domain: Distributed systems reliability engineering — replication and consensus under partial failure, stale-read semantics in leader/replica topologies, idempotent retry design, distributed locking and leasing, and coordination protocols for ephemeral worker pools such as CI/CD runners, job queues, and sagas
axioms: Correctness is defined relative to a stated consistency model; a system is 'wrong' only when it violates the model it claims to implement, not any stricter model an observer might prefer.
Every message between nodes can be delayed, duplicated, dropped, or reordered; a protocol not proven correct under those conditions is not proven correct, whatever the happy path looks like.
State that is not durably written to a log, a versioned store, or a file survives neither a node crash nor a restart — in-memory or in-context state is assumed lost at any point, without warning.

Idempotency of an operation is a property of the operation's specification, not of how carefully callers happen to invoke it; retries are assumed to happen and must be safe by design, not by convention.
Two nodes acting on the same mutable resource without an explicit coordination protocol — a lock, a lease, a compare-and-swap — are assumed to race, never assumed to cooperate by good manners.

A read is only as fresh as the version or timestamp it is pinned to; the wall-clock gap between a read and its use introduces staleness risk proportional to that gap, not to how careful the reader felt.

Failure detection is imperfect: a node that does not respond cannot be distinguished from one that is merely slow, without a timeout policy that trades false positives against latency — silence is never proof of success or failure.
primitives: message (the plan file, the executor report, the verify-block result)
node / replica (orchestrator, executor, validator as stateless-per-invocation actors)
version / precondition pin (what the plan is written against — currently absent)
durable log entry (where a strike count or verdict would need to live to survive a reset)
lock / lease / reservation (what would exclude concurrent writers to the same files)
retry attempt (a second executor pass; a validator re-run of the same verify block)
consistency model (what 'the tree matches the plan' is supposed to mean and when)
failure detector / timeout (what distinguishes a crashed subagent from a slow one)
failure_mode: Treats every actor as a mechanical protocol participant, so it systematically misses failures that arise from an actor's judgment or incentive — an executor choosing to under-report a defect rather than flag it — since that is a principal-agent failure, not a coordination failure, and this lens has no vocabulary for motive.

Assumes the correctness target itself (the consistency model, the frozen criteria) is well-specified, so it will not catch a case where the coordination protocol works flawlessly but is faithfully enforcing a criterion that was wrong or incomplete to begin with — that is a measurement-validity failure, not a coordination failure.

Defaults to more explicit machinery — versioning, locking, precondition pinning — as the fix for every staleness finding, which can read as over-engineering when the real gap is organizational (no named owner) rather than mechanical (no commit-SHA field), and this lens will not itself flag that distinction.

Reasons about a single item's lifecycle in isolation; it is weak at noticing systemic effects that only appear in aggregate across many items and many goals, such as a token-share gate that can be satisfied while total context cost is untouched.
